title: Fire is proper, not mere metaphor for wrath vs Puccius; Augustine on conflagration; Magius; starry heaven disputed
pass_a_gloss: We hold the ancients' sentence, resting on the sayings of Scripture by which we have already proved that this world will perish, to be preferable to the other. Augustine denies it, and with him the juniors. The most ancient fathers affirm it. But here it stands as controverted whether the starry heaven also stands as to be purged by fire. yet we love Augustine's modesty, who in the place praised judges that no one, so far as he himself knows, has known these things. But what that fire will stand as and whence it will come, Hieronymus Magius disputes in On the Burning belonging toward the World book 3: Then, he says, the figure belonging toward this world will pass away by the conflagration of worldly fires, just as it stood as done by the inundation of worldly waters in the flood. Hence Augustine (City of God book 20, chapter 16): yet that it stands as taken properly stands as argued by this, that it stands as said that as it formerly perished by water, so on that day it will perish by fire. But fire stands as thought to be taken by metaphor for divine wrath and judgment by Franciscus Puccius of Filidino, as Nicolaus Serarius the Mainz Jesuit notes (book 1 against Puccius, chapter 2, and book 2, chapter 2):
pass_b_english: But fire is thought to be taken by metaphor for divine wrath and judgment by Franciscus Puccius of Filidino, as Nicolaus Serarius the Mainz Jesuit notes (book 1 against Puccius, chapter 2, and book 2, chapter 2): yet that it is taken properly is argued by this, that it is said that as it formerly perished by water, so on that day it will perish by fire. Hence Augustine (City of God book 20, chapter 16): Then, he says, the figure of this world will pass away by the conflagration of worldly fires, just as it was done by the inundation of worldly waters in the flood.

But what that fire will be and whence it will come, Hieronymus Magius disputes in On the Burning of the World book 3: yet we love Augustine's modesty, who in the place praised judges that no one, so far as he himself knows, has known these things. But here it is controverted whether the starry heaven also is to be purged by fire. The most ancient fathers affirm it. Augustine denies it, and with him the juniors. We hold the ancients' sentence, resting on the sayings of Scripture by which we have already proved that this world will perish, to be preferable to the other.
source_text: Ignis vero per metaphoram pro ira & judicio divino accipi putatur a Francisco Puccio Filidino, ut notat Nicolaus Serarius Jesuita Moguntinus lib. 1. contra Puccium cap. 2. & lib. 2. cap. 2. sed proprie sumi, argumento est, quod dicatur, ut aqua prius interiit, ita in illo die igne periturum. Hinc Augustinus lib. 20. de C.D. cap. 16. Tunc, inquit, figura hujus mundi mundanorum ignium conflagratione praeteribit: sicut factum est mundanarum aquarum inundatione diluvii. Quis vero ille ignis sit futurus & unde venturus, disputat Hieronymus Magius lib. 3. de exustione mundi: at nos Augustini modestiam amamus, qui loco laudato, neminem, quod ipse sciat, novisse haec arbitratur. Est vero hic controversum, an etiam caelum sidereum igne sit expurgandum? Antiquissimi patres id affirmant. Negat Augustinus, & cum eo juniores. Nos antiquiorum sententiam dictis scripturae, quibus mundum hunc periturum esse jam probavimus, nixam, altera potiorem ducimus.
